beats.vo: Monday was the night Jonas brought cookies to his room. He ate them one by one in his bed, and they were delicious; they were very yummy.
Afterwards he had a pile of crumbs on his chest, which he brushed onto the covers, and went to bed. Only Jonas could not sleep. He tossed and turned.

All the cookie crumbs had traveled around his bed. Some were on sailboats, sailing near his feet. Others took cruise ships, partying by his pillow. Still others took helicopters, and the last were on motorcycles, zooming around by his feet.
And when he did finally fall asleep, his sleep was disturbed. It felt like the cookies had come to eat him.

cards.label: The cookies came to eat him

beats.vo: “That,” said Jonas, flinging his covers off in a jumbled mess, “is the last time I eat cookies in bed.”

cards.label: The last time I eat cookies in bed

beats.vo: On Tuesday, Jonas went to the beach. He had a great time crashing in the waves.
And it just so happened that some sand got into his shoes, and may have kinda, sorta ended up in bed — next to him, again.

This time Jonas really couldn’t sleep. The crumbs and the sand were doing jigs, meeting at bars, sweet talking, and taking each other home. “Leave me alone!” he cried. But they were too busy jamming to listen.

So Jonas shook out his blankets and stormed off in a huff. “I’m sleeping outside tonight!” “Wait for us,” a couple crumbs said, climbing onto his pillow. “Please! I don’t want you in my bed anymore,” he vowed through gritted teeth.

Finally the crumb and the sand near his ear stopped mid-jig and took pity on him. “Guys, let’s go.” And Jonas watched them pack up and go, and shed a single tear. “Goodnight, cookie crumbs. Goodnight, speckled sand,” he yawned, and dreamt of sleepy, sleepy sand.

Here's the honest truth. I didn't know I was a witch. Until one day I got so angry, I made something happen that I couldn't ignore.
Then I thought back through all those weird coincidences in my life that I thought had just been the universe trying to tell me something.
And I realized what I must have known all along. That I wasn't a bystander watching the strange things happen in my life.
But that I was the one causing them. Not literally causing every single thing to happen, but with my emotion, my intention, and my will.
Subtly changing the way my life had been flowing to match what I wanted.
I realized that I had wished for things and then gotten them, almost immediately.

projects.text: I've been thinking about how we're kind of a thought experiment that God was having. Imagine you would have thought experiment in the bath. You're thinking, what would happen if I ran into my ex? And then, like, I saw him and he had another girlfriend or something. So, in your mind, you plan all sorts of possibilities that might take place. But of course, you're controlling the people in your mind, and they do what you say, except sometimes they don't do exactly what you say, and you run the experiment to see what exactly would happen. in each set of circumstances. Like, suppose you looked really good that day or suppose you looked really bad. You run the experiment and you see the results. Now imagine that in that experiment, these people were actually real people. They had their own mind, and... They could make choices. that you didn't understand or didn't know about, and you could learn about them through these, you could learn about what would happen through these choices. This, I think, is what it's like when God created us. He created us in this world, where we can experience things, and it's like he's not there thinking about us, even though he actually is, because he wanted us to feel like we were really, Doing stuff and immersed in the experience to see what would happen. If you want to perform an accurate thought experiment, you can't get involved in the choices, right? Anyway. This got me thinking. What if you had a thought experiment, and then the people in your thought experiment actually came, they actually existed? And the world that you created in your head for the experiment was actually a real world. And it started acting independently of you. I think that is true, actually, to some extent, in that you can't 100% predict what will happen. But if you were as powerful as God, then you could actually create entire worlds and they would actually become physical. I think Jesus or somebody said this, that the weirdest thing or the most amazing thing is how the mental became physical. meaning that, Everything you see started as a thought. Someone else's thought.

projects.text: I don't know if these are exactly ideas I had last night. I've definitely had them before, but one of them was that I wanted to make, like, a video, I guess, talking about that thing that was written by that guy, Eckhart Toll, I think. Basically, the idea that... I sort of assumed, like, almost everyone else, I think, that it's best to believe, like, the worst, harshest thing, and that you shouldn't... get your hopes up. I'm not really sure where that idea came from, but it's so deeply ingrained in me that I absolutely never questioned it. I didn't want to be one of the fools that thought there was something magical or whatever. However, I did actually believe in God because I had seen that God existed through what I would consider empirical evidence. Though I wouldn't necessarily expect anyone to believe me, 'cause it's not something I could necessarily transfer anyway. When I read that part in Ecartoli, I actually thought, again, about whether it was necessary to... believe things in that way. And then I seems like as soon as I realized that that was its own, I guess you would call assumption or belief, that the thing you don't want to believe is probably the thing that's true. I was able to rip that out, and it left me in a very strange sort of magical place, standing on a magic carpet in the middle of nowhere, with Jesus above me, and God, and below me, everyone else, who thinks things that are... Well I don't know. The question is, I don't know what other beliefs I have that pertain to that. For example, I always assumed aliens weren't real, but I think they are real now. The other thing that I thought, or was it thinking about last night, was basically this idea about, like, rules, and... um... You know, you get Adam, then you get Moses. He's like, whoa, what are we doing? We need some rules, right? Then you finally get Jesus, and Jesus is like, actually, no, it's just like what's in your heart. So that's why Judaism has this belief that, basically, what you do is all that matters, and then Christianity is like, no, it's what's in your heart. So, like, faith in the 7 sins and virtues, they're all things that you think. I don't know if this is widely discussed, but I'm pretty sure you could be a glutton without actually overconsuming. And faith certainly isn't something that there's necessarily proof of. Well, in any case, a lot of the actual near death experiences, Jesus, as you as you can see from the review room, which might be portrayed as, like, a person in, like, one of those home theaters with just screens everywhere, almost like an octagonal room, 'cause screens on every wall, and they're just throwing popcorn into there, and it's landing in their mouth. That's why it's, like, kind of funny, but you see your life play out, and as God is often elegant, it's, like, rather than exactly being punished for your sins, 'cause how could you decide the exact punishment, an eye for an eye, you simply feel the feelings that the other person felt. That does seem like a rather elegant solution. But what it points at is that you've got a pipeline, you've got one, do whatever you want, then two, no, add some rules. Three. Actually, it's not about the rules, it's more about the underlying intention, because Jesus, there's that quote. He said, eat what you will, just heal the sick. But then in this last iteration or instance, it might be said or seen that it's none of those things. There's really no way you can decide your behavior. It's actually just how it ends up affecting people. For example, in one NDE, she said she was shown this boy that she rejected and how hurt it made him. Another one, a nurse. who she had mean thoughts about, and then another one at a checkout counter. She gave someone change, and they ended up working at a food bank. In another one, he helped this boy when he was little, and he had no idea that it would be important to him, but it was. So, if you're thinking, oh, I should just be a better person, it's not just about following rules. It's not just about having it in your heart. It's about actually doing better. And that seems like an impossible order. There's no program you can run on that. And so, really, I guess you need all three. You need to, you need to follow some, probably some roles, I guess, and have a good intention, but also be able to predict outcomes. And. I don't think that there's a program you can run for that.
